newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl ally sees few participants in euro at start.
newsitem.headline: Kohl ally sees few participants in euro at start.

text.p: A powerful ally of Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Saturday the number of countries taking part in European monetary union in 1999 will be small, but he hoped Britain would be among the founding members.

Wolfgang Schaeuble, leader of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) in the Bonn parliament, said in an interview with Der Spiegel newsweekly "the world will not end" for countries that do not immediately qualify for the single currency.

"We Germans should not say who we want to have and who we don't want to have," Schaeuble said when asked if Italy would qualify. "It is up to Italy to fulfil the criteria. But the world will not end for any country if it joins a year later."

In a separate interview, Gerhard Schroeder, premier in the state of Lower Saxony and a leading chancellor candidate for the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), stirred new fears against the euro by saying it would be weaker than the mark.

"Naturally the euro will be weaker than the mark," Schroeder told the newsweekly Focus. "If you put several weak currencies together with a few that are very strong, an absolutely strong currency cannot come out of that."

Schaeuble, an influential voice within the CDU on European affairs, said countries failing to meet the Maastrict requirements for EMU in 1997 will still have three years to reduce budget deficits or inflation rates and qualify for the euro before the new currency is in circulation.
"I believe the number of the Euro participants will not be all that large in 1999," he said.
Schaeuble said he was optimistic that Britain would take part in the euro from the outset. He said Britain was facing a difficult domestic political situation, but added that would eventually pass.
"I hope Britain will be there when the euro is launched," he said.
When asked if Spain and Italy would be among those in the EMU at the outset, Schaeuble said: "Let us wait and see what the results look like in the spring of 1998."
A survey by the INRA polling institute on Saturday found 54 percent of Germans surveyed felt the euro would bring them disadvantages while only 30 percent saw advantages.
Schaueble said he expected the prevailing scepticism towards the euro would fade once the euro is introduced.

"You could say on the one hand the success story of the mark is ending," he said. "Or you could say the success story of the mark will continue in the European monetary union. But then there is the danger that our French friends will read into that -- the euro is only an expanded D-mark."

But Schroeder, who regularly stands up well against Kohl in voter surveys and is the SPD candidate many say would pose the most serious threat to Kohl's hopes for reelection in 1998, said the lessons of German monetary union should not be forgotten.
Noting that west Germany transfers 200 billion marks each year to rebuild the eastern economy, Schroeder said similar costs could arise for the Germans with the EMU.
"The introduction of the euro could be similar," he said. "I really would have liked to know before the (German-German) monetary union how much it will cost us."
